where: Section 2, the four-part list of interrupt path
problem: The enable chain jumps from the peripheral's own enable bit straight to the CPU global mask. On the NVIC-based Cortex-M parts this chapter teaches, there is a third gate in between: the per-source enable in the controller (ISER). A student can set the UART enable, unmask the CPU, and still see no interrupt.
fix: Add a step: 'Controller enable: the request reaches the CPU only if that source's channel is enabled in the interrupt controller (ISER on the NVIC).' Then the global CPU mask comes last.

where: Section 2, last paragraph, and Q4 answer
problem: 'The flag stays set until software writes to it' is not true for every peripheral. Many UART, SPI and ADC flags clear when the data or status register is read, or clear on read-then-write. Presented as a rule, it will confuse a student whose UART flag clears by itself after reading the data register.
fix: Say: 'Most flags stay set until software clears them by writing to the status register; a few clear when the data register is read. Check the datasheet — the rule is that the source must be cleared before return, whichever way the part does it.'

problem: 'On ARM this is the I bit in the program status register' is true for classic ARM cores (CPSR I bit) but not for the Cortex-M cores that the rest of this chapter (NVIC, ISER, IPR) describes. Cortex-M has no settable I bit in xPSR; masking is done through PRIMASK (and BASEPRI for priority-level masking).
fix: Write: 'On classic ARM this is the I bit in the CPSR. On Cortex-M it is the PRIMASK register: CPSID i sets it, CPSIE i clears it, and BASEPRI can mask only sources below a chosen priority.'

where: Figure and Worked example 1, the statement that main makes no progress during latency
problem: The model treats the whole latency as dead time for the main program. But one of the latency causes listed in Section 3 is a software critical section, during which the main program is executing its own code, and detection time is also spent finishing a main-program instruction. The figure's blanket claim can mislead.
fix: Qualify it: 'This assumes the latency comes from higher-priority interrupt activity, so the main program truly stalls. If the latency comes from a critical section in the main code, the CPU is busy inside that section and the main program is making progress, though the ISR is still late.'
